name: Guambiano
confidence_why: Caudmont 1954 and Branks & Branks 1973, the only two first-hand phonologies of Guambía Namtrik, both report that stress has no fixed position in the word, differing only on whether it is provably contrastive (Branks & Branks give three near-minimal pairs; Caudmont found none), and no later study revisits the question.

catalog_quote: 1.6.—El acento. El acento tónico guambiano puede caer sobre cualquier sílaba de la palabra, pero no se ha podido probar su valor diferenciativo en contexto idéntico. Como el idioma contiene un alto porcentaje de palabras monosilábicas y como la mayoría de las palabras polisilábicas genuinamente indígenas se pueden dividir en elementos monosilábicos primitivos, hay que suponer que el acento está relacionado con la formación de palabras compuestas o con la derivación (raíz acentuada), porque su posición fluctuante no permite una interpretación demarcativa: meRapaší 'adelante!' atsimáy 'a la izquierda' ... purámpi 'mazorca' [purámbi] ... kisímbimera 'lágrimas' lamústekən 'poco' [lamústegən]

new_statements.quote: 5. Acento. Al nivel de la palabra el acento es contrastable; en la sílaba acentuada ocurre tono alto. Sin embargo son raros los pares mínimos que solo difieran por el acento. /wa'ʂɨ/ 'águila' /'waʂɨ/ 'arriba' /pa'¢ɨ/ 'estómago' /'pi¢ɨ/ 'leche' /wan'čɨtan/ 'el río bramaba' /wančɨ'pen/ 'mientras el río bramaba'. 6. Entonación. Hay un modelo básico de entonación; es del nivel de la frase. Un modelo de entonación más bien parejo viene desde el comienzo de la frase. El tono se eleva un poco en los acentos de las palabras y se eleva al máximo en el acento del verbo principal y luego normalmente cae agudamente al final del verbo, que está de ordinario al final de la frase.
new_statements.translation: 5. Stress. At the word level stress is contrastive; high tone occurs on the stressed syllable. However, minimal pairs that differ only by stress are rare. /wa'ʂɨ/ 'eagle' vs /'waʂɨ/ 'up/above'; /pa'¢ɨ/ 'stomach' vs /'pi¢ɨ/ 'milk'; /wan'čɨtan/ 'the river roared' vs /wančɨ'pen/ 'while the river roared'. 6. Intonation. There is one basic intonation pattern; it belongs to the phrase level. A rather even intonation pattern runs from the beginning of the phrase. Pitch rises a little on the stresses of the words and rises to its maximum on the stress of the main verb, then normally falls sharply at the end of the verb, which is ordinarily at the end of the phrase.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (webcat) codes Guambiano 'lexical' on Caudmont 1954 ('El acento tónico guambiano puede caer sobre cualquier sílaba de la palabra.. su posición fluctuante no permite una interpretación demarcativa'); the roster's entries rest on Gonzales Castaño 2019 (Totoró Namtrik; stress conditions /ɨ/ allophony, no placement rule). Branks & Branks 1973 agrees: stress is word-level contrastive, position not rule-governed, and it refines the picture with the phonetic cue (high tone on the stressed syllable), three near-minimal pairs, and the phrase-level intonation contour peaking on the main verb. It does not contradict Caudmont, though where Caudmont could not prove a distinctive value, Branks &…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) and its position is not given by any rule; the stressed syllable carries high pitch. Examples in the article show stress on final (/pae'lɨ/, /maom'pe/, /wančɨ'pen/), penultimate (/wan'čɨtan/, /po'moyta/) and initial (/'waʂɨ/, /'noimpe/) syllables. Minimal pairs exist but are rare. At phrase level pitch rises slightly on each word stress, peaks on the main-verb stress, then falls sharply at the phrase-final verb.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. Sec. 3 (printed p.44) notes that some C.C examples are marked with two stresses because they are really two equally stressed phonological words forming one phonological phrase, written as one word. Orthography key (p.56) marks stress with an acute over the vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the authors only note that minimal pairs differing solely by stress are rare.
new_statements.identity_note: Branks & Branks 1973 describe the Guambiano spoken on the western slopes of the Cordillera Central near Silvia, Cauca (5,000-7,000 speakers, data collected 1965-1969 with speakers from Pueblito), i.e. the Guambía variety of Namtrik; the roster's the verification source (Gonzales Castaño 2019) is the Totoró variety. The article calls the language 'Chibcha' following Castellví and Loukotka; Glottolog places it in Barbacoan.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources. Caudmont 1954 (catalog's deciding source) says stress can fall on any syllable and could not be shown to be distinctive in identical context; Branks & Branks 1973 say stress is contrastive at the word level but minimal pairs are rare, and give three (near-)minimal pairs. Both agree the position is not predictable by rule, so the catalog's 'lexical' coding stands; the only nuance is Caudmont's unproven distinctiveness versus Branks & Branks's rare minimal pairs, which is a difference in evidence, not in placement type. Gonzales Castaño 2019 (Totoró variety) is consistent (stress phonologically active, no placement rule).

sources.note: The only other primary phonology of guam1248; its chart lists 'Acento' as a suprasegmental phoneme, so its stress paragraph should say whether stress is contrastive (minimal pairs) or root-bound — exactly the point Caudmont 1954 leaves open ('no se ha podido probar su valor diferenciativo'; conjectured 'raíz acentuada'), which decides lexical vs set by morphology.
